sql_schemas: table leave_requests | fields: id, employee_id, leave_type_code, start_date, end_date, requested_days, reason, status, approver_id, approval_comment, submitted_at, decided_at, cancelled_by, cancelled_at, reverses_request_id | pk: id | fks: employee_id -> employees.id; leave_type_code -> leave_types.code; approver_id -> employees.id; cancelled_by -> employees.id; reverses_request_id -> leave_requests.id | indexes: reverses_request_id: NEW for GP-008 — the only way to find the reversal row that references an original, and the column the at-most-one-reversal guard reads before inserting; nullable, so the index is partial (WHERE reverses_request_id IS NOT NULL) and can carry a UNIQUE constraint to make double-reversal impossible at the storage layer; employee_id: role-scoped list/getById filtering (findByQuery binds employee_id = ANY($n) for EMPLOYEE/MANAGER visibility); status: findByQuery status filter and the APPROVED-only cancellation lookup; leave_type_code, start_date: leave-type + date-range list queries; start_date also drives the ORDER BY start_date DESC list ordering; employee_id, status: existing composite from the initial schema, retained for the common 'my requests in state X' access pattern; approver_id: approver-side lookups (who decided what); no new index needed beyond the FK; cancelled_by: canceller-side lookups; no new index needed beyond the FK

data_notes:
Persistence slice for GP-008 (approved leave reversal). Only ONE table changes: `leave_requests` gains the nullable `reverses_request_id` column (FK -> leave_requests.id) plus an index, delivered as a new knex migration (`migrations/<ts>_add_reverses_request_id_to_leave_requests.js`, `alterTable` up / `dropColumn` down) following the existing `20260913000001_add_password_hash_to_employees.js` convention. No SQL DDL is written here — the code agent generates the migration from this spec.

Tables defined exactly once and referenced by name elsewhere (unchanged by this feature, no new columns): `employees`, `leave_types`, `leave_policies`, `leave_balances`, `audit_logs`, `notifications`. Their specs are the ones already recorded in the initial schema and the reconciled architecture; this feature must not restate or alter them.

Read-model change: `LeaveRequest` gains `reversesRequestId: string | null` (15th field), `CreateLeaveRequestInput` stays `Omit<LeaveRequest,'id'>` so `create` supplies it (null for every non-reversal row), `PgLeaveRequestRepository.COLUMNS`/`LeaveRequestRow`/`mapRow` carry `reverses_request_id`, and `GET /leaves` / `GET /leaves/:id` therefore expose it — a client can tell the untouched APPROVED original from the new CANCELLED reversal. `UpdateLeaveRequestDto` deliberately does NOT gain `reversesRequestId`: the column is set only at insert time, never mutated, which is what keeps the reversal link immutable.

GP-008 immutability is enforced at the data-access layer by omission: the APPROVED cancellation path calls `repository.create` (new row) and never `repository.update` on the original, so status/approverId/approvalComment/decidedAt of the approved row cannot be touched. DRAFT/SUBMITTED cancellation keeps using `repository.update` in place, unchanged.

Balance release is unchanged in magnitude and happens exactly once: the APPROVED path reads the balance with `forUpdate = true` and issues exactly one `usedDays -= requestedDays` write inside the same transaction as the reversal insert; the DRAFT path still touches no balance row and the SUBMITTED path still releases `pendingDays` only. The audit record (AuditAction.CANCEL) and the requester notification are still written, now joined to the same transaction.

Two genuinely undecided points are recorded as openQuestions rather than silently asserted: (1) whether the exactly-once release is enforced by a partial UNIQUE index on `reverses_request_id` or only by an in-transaction service check; (2) what the reversal row carries in `requested_days`/dates/approver fields, which matters because `requested_days` is the canonical inclusive day count and any aggregate over non-cancelled rows must not double-count.

open_questions.question: Where is the "release exactly once" invariant enforced — a UNIQUE constraint on leave_requests.reverses_request_id, or a service-level findByReversesRequestId check inside the transaction?
open_questions.impact: Determines whether the migration adds a partial UNIQUE index (making a second reversal of the same APPROVED row impossible at the storage layer, surfacing as a 409/23505) or only a plain index (leaving the guard to application code, which is racy under concurrent cancellations of the same request). It also decides whether the repository must translate a unique-violation into ConflictError.
candidate_options: Partial UNIQUE index on reverses_request_id (WHERE reverses_request_id IS NOT NULL) + service pre-check; repository maps 23505 to ConflictError
Plain non-unique index only; the service's findByReversesRequestId check inside the transaction is the sole guard
Partial UNIQUE index only, no service pre-check; rely on the constraint and map the violation to ConflictError

open_questions.question: What does the NEW CANCELLED reversal row carry in requested_days, start_date, end_date, approver_id, approval_comment and decided_at?
open_questions.impact: requested_days is the canonical inclusive day count and is the value the balance release is computed from; if the reversal row copies the original's requested_days, any future aggregate that sums requested_days over non-cancelled rows must exclude CANCELLED rows or it will double-count the leave. approver_id/decided_at/approval_comment on the reversal row decide whether the reversal looks like it was itself approved.
candidate_options: Copy start_date/end_date/requested_days/leave_type_code/employee_id from the original; set approver_id, approval_comment, decided_at, submitted_at to null (the reversal was never approved)
Copy the dates and leave_type_code but persist requested_days = 0 on the reversal row (the reversal releases, it does not request)
Copy every field of the original except id/status/cancelled_by/cancelled_at/reverses_request_id, including approver_id and decided_at

transaction_contract: This feature has multi-step writes that must be atomic (insert the reversal row + release the balance + write the audit record + notify), so a transaction contract applies. It reuses the existing platform contract, unchanged: the SERVICE owns the unit of work. `LeaveService.cancel` wraps the whole operation in `IUnitOfWork.withTransaction` (`PgUnitOfWork`: acquires a `PoolClient` from the shared pool, BEGIN, runs the callback, COMMIT on resolve / ROLLBACK on throw, always releases). Every repository/service method that must join the caller's transaction takes an OPTIONAL trailing `client?: PoolClient` parameter and falls back to the shared pool when omitted — `ILeaveRepository.create`, `ILeaveRepository.findByReversesRequestId`, `ILeaveRepository.update`, `IBalanceRepository.findByKey`/`update`, `IAuditService.record`, `INotificationService.create`. The service passes the transaction client to each call in order: (1) `findByReversesRequestId(originalId, client)` guard, (2) `balanceRepository.findByKey(..., client, forUpdate = true)` row lock, (3) `balanceRepository.update(balanceId, { usedDays: usedDays - requestedDays }, client)` — the single release, (4) `repository.create(reversalRow, client)` — the new CANCELLED row, (5) `auditService.record(CANCEL, client)`, (6) `notificationService.create(..., client)`. Repositories never open BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK; only `PgUnitOfWork` does. The DRAFT/SUBMITTED paths keep the same shape but substitute `repository.update` in place of steps 1 and 4. Read paths (`list`, `getById`) open no transaction and forward no client.
